tips.title: Three figures, from north, clockwise
tips.body: Every bearing needs all three. **From north**, **clockwise**, and **three figures**, so $70°$ is written $070°$. Dropping the leading zero is the cheapest mark to lose in the whole topic.

tips.title: The word from tells you where to stand
tips.body: *The bearing of B **from** A* is measured **at A**, with the north line drawn **at A**. Underline the word *from* and its letter before you draw anything: half the errors in this topic are measuring at the wrong end.

tips.title: Let the range pick the rule
tips.body: For a back bearing, do not memorise which way. A bearing must lie between $000°$ and $360°$, so try adding $180°$: if the answer goes over $360$, subtract instead. $250 + 180 = 430$ is impossible, so it must be $250 - 180 = 070°$.

tips.title: The turn is not the angle in the triangle
tips.body: Subtracting two bearings gives the **turn** at the corner. The angle **inside** the triangle is $180°$ minus that turn. They agree only at $90°$, which is why a right-angle example hides the difference. Put the interior angle into the cosine rule, never the turn.

steps.title: What a bearing is, exactly
steps.body:
A **bearing** is a direction, and it has three rules that must all hold. An answer breaking any one of them loses the mark even when the number is right.

1. Measured from **north**.
2. Measured **clockwise**.
3. Written with **three figures**, so $70°$ is written $070°$.

North is always drawn as a vertical line at the point you are measuring **from**. That is the part people skip: a bearing *of B from A* is measured at **A**, with north drawn at **A**.

So the phrase to read carefully is *the bearing of X **from** Y*. The word *from* tells you where to stand and where to draw north.

A table of eight compass directions with their three figure bearings

check.prompt: Write a bearing of 70 degrees correctly.
check.solution: Bearings always take **three figures**, so $70°$ is written **070°**.

steps.title: Back bearings
steps.body:
If the bearing of B from A is $070°$, what is the bearing of A from B? That is the **back bearing**, and it is the return journey.

The rule is simple arithmetic:

- If the bearing is **less than $180°$**, **add** $180°$.
- If it is **$180°$ or more**, **subtract** $180°$.

Either way the answer stays between $000°$ and $360°$, which is the check that you picked the right one.

steps.text: Now the reverse: $250°$ is more than $180°$, so **subtract**

steps.text: Adding 180 to 250 would give 430°, which is impossible, so the choice of rule is forced

steps.title: Scale drawings
steps.body:
A **scale** says how a length on paper relates to a length in real life. Two forms appear.

- **A statement**: *1 cm represents 5 km*. Multiply to go from paper to real, divide to come back.
- **A ratio**: *1 : 25,000*. Both sides are in the **same unit**, so 1 cm on the map is 25,000 cm in real life, and you convert afterwards.

The ratio form is where marks are lost, because the answer comes out in centimetres and has to be converted.

$7 \times 5 = 35$ km
Going back: a 40 km road would be $40 \div 5 = 8$ cm on the map
An 18 km road would be $18 \div 5 = 3.6$ cm

steps.title: Drawing and measuring accurately
steps.body:
A construction question is marked on **accuracy**, usually to within $2°$ and $2$ mm. That makes the method matter as much as the answer.

The order that works:

1. Draw a **north line** at the point you are measuring from, straight up the page.
2. Put the protractor's centre on that point, with $0°$ along the north line.
3. Measure **clockwise** to the bearing given.
4. Draw the line **long enough**, then mark the scaled distance along it with a ruler.

Leave the north lines and the construction marks on the page. An examiner cannot give method marks for working that has been rubbed out.

steps.title: The new north line at every point
steps.body:
The single biggest error in bearings questions is measuring the second leg from the **first** north line.

Every bearing is measured from the north line at the point you are **standing at**. So a journey with two legs needs **two** north lines: one at the start, one at the turning point. They are parallel, because north is north everywhere on the page.

That parallelism is also what makes back bearings work, though not quite in the obvious way. Two back bearings **differ** by $180°$; they do not add to it, since $070 + 250 = 320$. The co-interior pair is not the bearings themselves but the two angles between each north line and the line $AB$. With a bearing of $070°$, those angles are $70°$ at A and $110°$ at B, which do add to $180°$. Measuring that $110°$ clockwise from north at B gives $360 - 110 = 250°$, the back bearing.

steps.title: Your turn: draw it, then read it
steps.body:
A boat leaves port A and sails **30 km on a bearing of 060°** to B, then **40 km on a bearing of 150°** to C.

1. Work out both lengths on paper at a scale of 1 cm to 5 km.
2. Draw the journey, with a north line at **both** A and B.
3. Measure AC and convert it to kilometres.
4. Work out the bearing of A from B, and of C from B.

For the third one, notice the angle between the two legs before you measure: $150 - 60$ is worth calculating.

check.prompt: A boat sails 30 km on a bearing of 060°, then 40 km on 150°. The turn between the legs is a right angle. How far is it from the start, in km?
check.solution: The bearings differ by $150 - 60 = 90°$, so the legs meet at a right angle and Pythagoras applies: $\sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = \sqrt{900 + 1600} = \sqrt{2500} = 50$ km.

steps.title: Going deeper: when to calculate instead of drawing
steps.body:
A question that says *draw a scale diagram* wants a drawing, measured with a ruler and protractor, and marks accuracy. A question that gives distances and bearings but does **not** say draw is usually asking you to **calculate**, and the trigonometry topics supply the tools.

**Finding the angle inside the triangle.** Subtracting the bearings gives the **turn** at the corner, which is not the same as the angle inside the triangle. The angle at B is $180°$ **minus** the turn. Here the turn is $150 - 60 = 90°$, so the angle at B is $180 - 90 = 90°$ as well: a right angle is the one case where the turn and the interior angle agree. **Pythagoras** then gives the direct distance: $\sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50$ km. No drawing needed, and no measurement error.

**When it is not a right angle**, take care. Legs on $060°$ then $100°$ turn through only $40°$, but the angle inside the triangle is $180 - 40 = 140°$. Put the **interior** angle into the **cosine rule**, never the turn: using $40°$ there flips the sign of the cosine term and gives the wrong side. A bearing question at the top of the paper is often a triangle question in disguise.

**Going back to a bearing.** Having found an angle inside the triangle, you still have to turn it into a bearing measured clockwise from north at the right point. Draw the north line and work round: that last step is where calculated answers lose marks.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **bearing** is measured **from north**, **clockwise**, and written with **three figures**: $070°$, not $70°$.
- *The bearing of X **from** Y* is measured at **Y**, with north drawn at Y.
- **Back bearing**: add $180°$ if the bearing is under $180°$, subtract $180°$ if it is over. The answer must stay between $000°$ and $360°$.
- The back bearing rule comes from **co-interior angles** on the two parallel north lines: the angles to $AB$ are $70°$ and $110°$, and measuring the $110°$ clockwise gives $250°$.
- Every leg of a journey needs its **own north line** at its starting point.
- **Scale as a statement**: paper to real multiply, real to paper divide.
- **Scale as a ratio** 1 : 25,000: both sides are the same unit, so the answer comes out in centimetres and must be converted.
- Accuracy in a drawing is marked to about $2°$ and $2$ mm, so leave the construction lines on the page.
- **Subtract the bearings** to find the angle inside the triangle, then use Pythagoras, the cosine rule or the sine rule.
- This journey: legs of 6 cm and 8 cm, meeting at $90°$, a direct distance of 50 km.

questions.prompt: A boat sails 30 km from A on a bearing of 060° to B, then 40 km on a bearing of 150° to C. Without drawing, find the direct distance from A to C, and explain why your method works.
questions.solution: Subtracting the bearings gives one hundred and fifty minus sixty, that is ninety degrees, and that is the turn at B rather than the angle inside the triangle. The angle inside is one hundred and eighty minus the turn, which here is also ninety degrees, because a right angle is the one case where the two coincide. Since the angle at B is a right angle, the triangle A B C is right angled and Pythagoras applies. A C squared equals thirty squared plus forty squared, which is nine hundred plus one thousand six hundred, that is two thousand five hundred. Taking the square root gives fifty, so the direct distance from A to C is fifty kilometres. Calculating rather than drawing avoids any measurement error, so the answer is exact rather than within a tolerance.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The angle at B.** Subtracting the bearings gives the **turn**: $150 - 60 = 90°$. The angle **inside** the triangle is $180°$ minus that turn, so $180 - 90 = \mathbf{90°}$ as well. A right angle is the one case where the two are the same.

**A right angle means Pythagoras.**

$$AC^2 = 30^2 + 40^2 = 900 + 1600 = 2500$$

$$AC = \sqrt{2500} = \mathbf{50} \text{ km}$$

**Why calculate rather than draw?** A scale drawing is marked within about 2 mm, so it can only ever be close. Calculating gives the distance **exactly**, with no measurement error.

questions.prompt: Explain the three rules a bearing must follow, and describe how to find the bearing of A from B when you know the bearing of B from A.
questions.solution: A bearing must be measured from north, must be measured clockwise, and must be written with three figures, so a bearing of seventy degrees is written zero seven zero. To find the bearing of A from B when you know the bearing of B from A, add one hundred and eighty if the bearing you know is less than one hundred and eighty, and subtract one hundred and eighty if it is one hundred and eighty or more. Choosing the right one is forced by the fact that a bearing must lie between zero and three hundred and sixty degrees, so whichever operation keeps the answer in that range is the correct one. The rule works because the north line at A is parallel to the north line at B, which makes the two bearings co-interior angles, and co-interior angles on parallel lines add to one hundred and eighty degrees.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The three rules.** A bearing is measured **from north**, **clockwise**, and written with **three figures**: $70°$ becomes $070°$.

**Finding the back bearing.**

- Bearing **under $180°$** → **add** $180°$
- Bearing **$180°$ or more** → **subtract** $180°$

You never need to remember which: a bearing must lie between $000°$ and $360°$, so only one of the two keeps the answer valid. Adding 180 to $250°$ gives $430°$, which is impossible.

**Why it works.** North at A and north at B are **parallel**, so the two bearings are **co-interior angles**, and co-interior angles on parallel lines add to $180°$.

examTechnique.body:
Underline the word *from* in the question and the letter after it. That tells you where to stand and where the north line goes, and it prevents the commonest error in the topic before you have drawn anything.

Write three figures every single time, even when the bearing is small. An answer of 70° where 070° was wanted is a lost mark for nothing.

Convert all the distances before you pick up a ruler. Doing the arithmetic mid-drawing is where scale errors creep in.

Draw a fresh north line at every point you measure from, and leave it on the page. Leave the protractor marks and construction lines too: an examiner cannot credit working that has been rubbed out.

When the question does not say *draw*, subtract the bearings to find the angle inside the triangle and calculate instead. A difference of 90° means Pythagoras; anything else means the cosine rule.

Check any bearing you give is between 000° and 360°. If it is not, you have added when you should have subtracted.
examinerErrors: Writing 70° instead of 070°, so a correct direction loses the mark.
Measuring the bearing at the wrong end, by ignoring the word from.
Measuring anticlockwise, which gives 360 minus the right answer.
Measuring the second leg from the first north line instead of drawing a new one.
Adding 180 to a bearing over 180, giving an impossible answer above 360.
With a ratio scale, giving the answer in centimetres when kilometres were asked for.
Rubbing out the construction lines, so the method marks cannot be given.
Drawing when the question wanted a calculation, and losing accuracy to measurement.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer underlines the word from, draws a north line at every point it measures from, and writes every bearing with three figures. It converts all the distances before drawing and leaves the construction marks on the page. Given distances and bearings with no instruction to draw, it subtracts the bearings to get the angle in the triangle and calculates, choosing Pythagoras for a right angle and the cosine rule otherwise, and says why calculating is more accurate than measuring. It checks that every bearing it gives lies between 000° and 360°, and can explain the back bearing rule as co-interior angles on parallel north lines rather than as a fact to memorise.
